posts.headline: 3 Concerts in 12 Days
posts.prose: I don't know what got into me in July 2023, but I saw 3 shows across 3 different genres in 12 days without once feeling like I was overdoing it. Foals at The Belasco on the 18th, UB40 at Peacock Theater on the 21st, X at Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa on the 30th — indie rock, reggae, and punk, all inside a single Los Angeles summer. There's something about that stretch that still makes me smile: I went from the close, sweaty energy of The Belasco to an amphitheatre in Orange County without stopping to ask whether any of it made sense as a playlist. It didn't, and that was exactly the point.

social.hook: Three genres, three venues, twelve days — and not once did I question the logic.
social.caption: July 2023: Foals, UB40, and X across twelve days without a coherent playlist in sight. That was entirely the point.
beats: July 2023: three shows in twelve days, three genres, two counties — and it never felt like too much.
Foals at The Belasco on the 18th: close, sweaty, the room pressing in from every side.
UB40 at Peacock Theater on the 21st — reggae in the middle of an LA summer felt exactly right.
X at Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa on the 30th: punk under an open Orange County sky.
Indie rock, reggae, punk — no through line, no apology. The archive holds all three.

posts.headline: Social Distortion — 1.4 Years Before Born to Kill
posts.prose: Punk rock has always been about the song before the studio catches up, and at The Belasco in Los Angeles on December 5, 2024, I heard four tracks from *Born to Kill* a full 519 days before the record existed in anyone's hands. Four songs — "Tonight," "Over You," "The Way Things Were," and the title track itself — dropped into an 18-song set like they'd always belonged there, which, knowing Social Distortion, they probably had for years already. That's the thing about a band formed in 1979: they don't audition new material, they road-test it, and the crowd at The Belasco had no idea they were the test.

social.hook: Four songs from an album that wouldn't exist for another 519 days.
social.caption: Four tracks from Born to Kill landed in an 18-song set before the record existed. The Belasco crowd had no idea they were the test.
beats: The Belasco, December 5, 2024 — Social Distortion playing an 18-song set in their own backyard.
Four of those songs had no release date, no album, no existence outside the live room.
'Tonight,' 'Over You,' 'The Way Things Were,' and the title track — dropped in like they'd always been there.
A band formed in 1979 doesn't audition new material. They road-test it. The crowd didn't know.
Born to Kill was still 519 days away. The people in that room heard it first.

posts.headline: "Notorious": Nile Rodgers and Duran Duran, 39 Years Apart
posts.prose: "Notorious" is a song with two authors in a sense — Duran Duran wrote it, but Nile Rodgers produced it, and his fingerprints are all over that bassline. I heard Duran Duran play it at Irvine Meadows in July 1987, and then 39 years later I watched Rodgers claim it fully at the Pacific Amphitheatre, playing it as his own with complete justification. Two different Southern California venues, two different summers, the same song landing with the same authority both times. I didn't plan that symmetry — it just accumulated in my ticket stubs, waiting for me to notice.

social.hook: 39 years between ticket stubs, same song, same authority
social.caption: Nile Rodgers played 'Notorious' at the Pacific Amphitheatre as if he'd always owned it — and in every way that matters, he had. That bassline was his fingerprint long before I connected the two stubs.
beats: Duran Duran played 'Notorious' at Irvine Meadows in July 1987. I was there.
Nile Rodgers produced that record — his fingerprints are all over the bassline.
39 years later he played it at the Pacific Amphitheatre, claiming it fully and without apology.
Two Southern California venues, two different summers, the same song landing with the same authority both times.
I didn't plan the symmetry. It just accumulated in my ticket stubs, waiting for me to notice.

posts.headline: July 31: 40 Years Since The Art of Noise
posts.prose: I drove down to the Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa on July 31, 1986, genuinely unsure what a live Art of Noise show would even look like — they were a studio project, built from samples and synthesizers, and the stage setup felt more like a science experiment than a concert. It's been 40 years since that night, and I still remember the disorientation of watching music that seemed to exist only on record suddenly fill an outdoor amphitheatre with actual air and heat and crowd noise. They had already released *(Who's Afraid of) The Art of Noise?* by then, and hearing those fractured rhythms in the open California summer felt genuinely strange in the best way. Some shows you attend; that one attended me.

social.hook: A studio project built from samples — and suddenly it was filling outdoor air.
social.caption: Art of Noise in 1986 was a science experiment more than a concert. Forty years later I still can't explain exactly what I witnessed that night.
beats: I drove to Costa Mesa with no idea what a live Art of Noise show could possibly be.
They were a studio project — samples, synthesizers, no conventional band to stand behind.
The stage setup looked like a science experiment. Then the fractured rhythms hit open California air.
*(Who's Afraid of) The Art of Noise?* was already out. Hearing it outdoors felt genuinely strange.
Some shows you attend. That one attended me.

posts.headline: Pacific Amphitheatre: 16 Shows Over 5 Decades
posts.prose: I was 16 years old the first time I walked into the Pacific Amphitheatre, catching Tears For Fears in the summer of 1985 — right in the thick of the *Songs from the Big Chair* era. Thirty-nine years later, I closed the loop with The English Beat in July 2024, and somewhere in between I fit in 14 more nights at that Costa Mesa bowl, from the Beach Boys to Run-DMC to UB40. Sixteen shows across 5 decades at the same venue feels less like a habit and more like a relationship. I didn't plan any of this, which somehow makes it better.

social.caption: I was 16 the first time I walked into the Pacific Amphitheatre for Tears For Fears in 1985. Thirty-nine years later, The English Beat closed the loop — with 14 more nights in between.
beats: Summer 1985: I was 16, Songs from the Big Chair was everywhere, and the Pacific Amphitheatre was brand new to me.
Fourteen more nights followed — the Beach Boys, Run-DMC, UB40, Sting, Garbage, and others filling the decades between.
The same Costa Mesa bowl held all of it: ska, punk, pop, hip-hop, and a Stray Cats set I still think about.
July 2024, The English Beat closed the loop. Thirty-nine years between first show and sixteenth.
I never planned to make this place a through-line. That's probably why it became one.

posts.headline: July 16: 40 Years Since Beach Boys
posts.prose: I was at the Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa on July 16, 1986 — 40 years ago today — and I still remember the way the summer air felt when the opening notes hit. The Beach Boys had been together 25 years by then, and somehow they made those harmonies sound like they were being invented right there in front of me. It was one of my earliest entries in what would become decades of concert-going, and I had no idea I was starting something. Forty years later, that night still feels like the right place to have begun.

beats: July 16, 1986: summer air, an open-air amphitheatre, and a band already 25 years deep into those harmonies.
It was one of my earliest concert entries — I had no idea I was opening an archive that would run for decades.
Something about hearing those voices live made the songs feel invented on the spot, not performed from memory.
Forty years on, that night still reads like the right place to have started.

posts.headline: House of Blues Anaheim: 6 Shows Over 3 Decades
posts.prose: I still think about walking into House of Blues Anaheim for the first time in August 2003 to see Joe Jackson — an artist who'd been making records since before I probably knew what a record was. Six shows across three decades at that same room, from that night with Joe Jackson all the way to Social Distortion in December 2022, with Streetlight Manifesto, Future Islands, and Royal Blood filling the years in between. Five artists who share almost nothing sonically, which tells me the venue was doing something right. Somehow a club in Anaheim became a quiet constant in my concert life, and I never quite planned it that way.

social.hook: Five artists, almost nothing in common, one room that kept pulling me back.
social.caption: Six shows at the same Anaheim club across three decades, starting in August 2003. I never planned it as a series — the room just kept earning the return.

Five artists who share almost nothing sonically. That range tells me the venue was doing something right.
The last of the six came in December 2022. Nearly twenty years between the first night and the last.
I never set out to make it a series. Somehow a club in Anaheim became a quiet constant anyway.

posts.headline: Ziggy Marley: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: One show in 36 years of concert-going — just Ziggy Marley, Mesa Amphitheatre, September 1988, and then nothing. I've seen artists dozens of times, built whole chapters of this archive around them, but somehow Ziggy never crossed my path again despite releasing records like *Rebellion Rises* and *Love Is My Religion* that I genuinely love. That single 1988 date sits in the archive like a polaroid found in a jacket pocket — vivid, a little mysterious, and making me wonder how I let 36 years slip by without a second show.

social.hook: One show in 36 years, and I still haven't figured out how that happened.
social.caption: Ziggy Marley crossed my path exactly once in 36 years of concert-going. That 1988 night sits in the archive like a polaroid found in a jacket pocket — vivid and a little mysterious.

September 1988, Mesa Amphitheatre. A single polaroid in the archive, vivid and unexplained.
Records I genuinely love — Rebellion Rises, Love Is My Religion — and still no second show.

posts.headline: June 21: 35 Years Since Jimmy Buffett
posts.prose: I was at Irvine Meadows on June 21, 1991 — 35 years ago today — and I remember the sun going down over the amphitheater in a way that felt almost staged, like the sky was in on the joke. Jimmy Buffett had been playing that Southern California crowd like a warm ocean current, and somewhere between *Changes In Latitudes* and *Songs You Know By Heart*, the whole place stopped being a concert and started being a backyard party for 15,000 strangers. I didn't own a single piece of Parrothead gear, but I understood it completely by the end of the night. Some shows teach you why a fanbase exists — this was one of them.

social.caption: Some shows teach you why a fanbase exists. I walked in skeptical and walked out understanding every bit of it.

Buffett worked that Southern California crowd like a warm ocean current all night long.

15,000 strangers. No Parrothead gear on me. Complete understanding by the final song.
Thirty-five years on, I still think of it as the show that explained a fanbase.

posts.headline: No Doubt: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: Here's something that stopped me cold when I was flipping through my oldest entries: I saw No Doubt at Disneyland in March 1988 — just two years after they formed — opening alongside The Nylons in Anaheim before virtually anyone outside Southern California knew their name. That's the only No Doubt entry in my entire archive, which means I caught them exactly once, at what had to be one of their earliest public performances, and never crossed paths with them again through *Tragic Kingdom*, *Rock Steady*, or any of the singles years. The fact that my sole sighting happened at a theme park in 1988 is the kind of detail I couldn't have invented.

social.hook: One sighting. A theme park. Two years after they formed.
social.caption: My only No Doubt entry in the entire archive is from 1988 — before anyone outside Southern California knew their name. Everything that followed, I missed.

March 1988: they were two years old as a band, opening alongside The Nylons at a theme park in Anaheim.
Virtually no one outside Southern California knew who they were yet — Tragic Kingdom was still years away.
I never crossed paths with them again. One accidental early sighting, then nothing — that's the whole file.

posts.headline: Garbage — Days Before Late Registration Dropped
posts.prose: In July 2005, hip-hop was about to get its most orchestral moment yet — Kanye West's Late Registration would drop just 34 days after I saw Garbage at Pacific Amphitheatre. I remember thinking how perfectly Shirley Manson's electronic-rock theatrics felt that summer, all moody synthesizers and guitar distortion. What I didn't know was that across town, Kanye was putting finishing touches on an album that would blend hip-hop with string arrangements in ways that echoed Garbage's own genre-blending DNA from the '90s. Sometimes the musical zeitgeist reveals itself in hindsight.

social.hook: 34 days before Late Registration, the zeitgeist was already in the air.
social.caption: I saw Garbage on July 27, 2005, not yet knowing Kanye was finishing Late Registration across town. The genre-blending instinct was everywhere that summer, if you knew where to listen.
beats: July 27, 2005: Shirley Manson brings moody synthesizers and guitar distortion to Pacific Amphitheatre.
Thirty-four days later, Kanye West's Late Registration would arrive and reframe what genre-blending could mean.
Garbage had been doing their own version of that instinct since the '90s — electronics, rock, tension held together.
The connection only became visible in hindsight. That's what the archive is for.

posts.headline: Run DMC: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: I caught Run DMC exactly once in my entire concert history — June 20, 1987 at Pacific Amphitheatre with the Beastie Boys opening. This was right in their Raising Hell era, when both acts were ascending rapidly, and somehow I never managed to see either of them again despite decades of concertgoing. Looking back, that single show captured lightning in a bottle: two pioneering hip-hop acts sharing a stage just as the genre was breaking into the mainstream. I can't believe I let 37 years pass without another Run DMC sighting.

social.hook: One night, two acts, 37 years of no second chance.
social.caption: I saw Run-D.M.C. exactly once in 37 years of concertgoing, and the Beastie Boys were opening. That single night has never stopped feeling like the one I couldn't afford to miss twice.
beats: June 20, 1987: both acts were ascending fast, and somehow I only had one ticket to spend on either of them.
Raising Hell was the record in the air that night — hip-hop pushing hard at the edge of the mainstream.
The Beastie Boys opened. Two pioneering acts on the same bill, and I was there for all of it.
I never saw Run-D.M.C. again. Not once in the 37 years that followed.
The full account is in the archive. One show. No second chance.

posts.headline: Sting — Days After Nevermind Dropped
posts.prose: Nevermind hit shelves on September 24th, 1991, and within days the entire rock landscape had shifted — yet there I was on October 4th, just 10 days later, watching Sting perform his polished pop-rock at Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa. I remember thinking how surreal it felt to be hearing "Fields of Gold" while the radio was still figuring out what to do with "Smells Like Teen Spirit." The timing captures this perfect moment when the old guard was still touring their greatest hits, completely unaware that the ground had already moved beneath them.

social.hook: Ten days after Nevermind dropped, the old guard hadn't heard the news yet.
social.caption: Sting played Pacific Amphitheatre ten days after Nevermind changed everything. The ground had already moved; nobody on stage knew it yet.
beats: Nevermind hit shelves September 24th, 1991. I was at this show ten days later.
Radio was still figuring out what to do with 'Smells Like Teen Spirit' that night.
Meanwhile, polished pop-rock filled the amphitheatre, unhurried and unaware.
That gap — ten days, two worlds — is exactly what this archive exists to hold.

posts.headline: Siouxsie and the Banshees — Days After Achtung Baby Dropped
posts.prose: December 1991 was the month U2 shattered expectations with Achtung Baby, trading earnest anthems for industrial textures and irony — and just 33 days after that seismic shift dropped, I caught Siouxsie and the Banshees at the Universal Amphitheater. Here were two bands who'd spent the '80s proving that reinvention was survival, but Siouxsie had been mining that dark, electronic-tinged territory since 1976 while Bono was still figuring out how to be mysterious. Watching her command that stage in the shadow of U2's supposed "breakthrough" felt like a reminder of who'd been doing the real pioneering work all along.

social.hook: Achtung Baby was 33 days old. Someone had been doing this since 1976.
social.caption: Siouxsie and the Banshees took the Universal Amphitheater stage 33 days after Achtung Baby reframed what rock reinvention could mean. She'd been working that dark, electronic-tinged ground since 1976.
beats: December 21, 1991: Achtung Baby was five weeks old and everywhere you looked.
U2's pivot to industrial textures felt seismic — unless you'd been paying attention to Siouxsie since 1976.
She didn't acknowledge the comparison. She didn't have to. The stage said it.
Watching her that night reordered the story of who pioneered what, and when.

posts.headline: April 15: 40 Years Since Blancmange
posts.prose: I saw Blancmange at Crawford Hall in Irvine 40 years ago today, and I can still picture Neil Arthur's theatrical gestures as they played through songs from Happy Families. This was during their synth-pop peak, when their blend of electronic beats and Arthur's distinctive vocals felt like the future of pop music. Crawford Hall was an intimate venue for a band that was getting significant radio play, making it feel like catching lightning in a bottle. Looking back, that April night in 1986 captured a specific moment when British new wave was reshaping American college radio.

social.hook: Neil Arthur's gestures made a synth-pop show feel like theater.
social.caption: Blancmange packed Crawford Hall while Happy Families was on college radio. Forty years on, I still see Neil Arthur conducting the room.
beats: April 1986: Blancmange were getting real radio play, yet Crawford Hall kept it close enough to feel personal.
They played through Happy Families — electronic beats and Arthur's voice cutting through a room that size.
Arthur's theatrical gestures turned a synth-pop set into something closer to performance art.
British new wave was reshaping American college radio that spring, and this night was the proof.
Forty years later, the detail that stays is how small the room was for a band that big.

posts.headline: April 12: 40 Years Since The Alarm
posts.prose: I remember standing in that UCLA crowd 40 years ago today, watching The Alarm tear through their set with an intensity that felt almost desperate. Mike Peters had this way of leaning into the microphone like he was trying to pull every person in the venue into whatever urgent message he was delivering, and at 15, I was completely susceptible to that kind of raw conviction. They were still riding high on Strength, and you could feel the band's belief that rock music could still change the world—a notion that seemed both naive and absolutely necessary in 1986. Forty years later, I still get that same surge of adrenaline when "68 Guns" comes on shuffle.

social.hook: I was 15, and Mike Peters made me believe rock could change the world.
social.caption: Forty years ago I stood in that UCLA crowd at 15, completely undone by The Alarm's conviction. That feeling still hits every time '68 Guns' comes on shuffle.
beats: April 12, 1986: I was 15 years old and had no defenses against that kind of raw urgency.
Mike Peters leaned into the mic like he was physically pulling each person toward whatever he needed to say.
The band was still riding Strength, and the room felt the weight of their belief that rock music mattered.
The idea that music could change the world seemed naive and absolutely necessary at the same time.
Forty years on, '68 Guns' still delivers that same surge of adrenaline when it hits shuffle.

posts.headline: The Brian Setzer Orchestra: 22 Years of Shows
posts.prose: I remember discovering The Brian Setzer Orchestra at the Hard Rock Cafe in Newport Beach back in 1995, when swing revival was just starting to bubble up from the underground. That first show hooked me on Brian's rockabilly-meets-big-band sound, and I ended up catching them 4 times across 22 years, from that intimate club gig all the way to the Warner Theatre in DC in 2017. Four different venues, three different decades, but always that same electric energy when Brian strapped on his hollow-body Gretsch and the 17-piece orchestra kicked into high gear. There's something deeply satisfying about following an artist long enough to watch both of you age into the music.

social.hook: Four shows. Three decades. One hollow-body Gretsch.
social.caption: I caught The Brian Setzer Orchestra 4 times across 22 years, from a club in Newport Beach to the Warner Theatre in DC. There's something to be said for aging into the music alongside an artist.
beats: Spring 1995: swing revival was still underground when I walked into the Hard Rock Cafe in Newport Beach.
One night with a 17-piece orchestra and a hollow-body Gretsch, and I was hooked for the next two decades.
Four venues, three decades — the last stop was the Warner Theatre in Washington DC in 2017.
Some artists you see once. Others you follow long enough that the music starts to feel like shared history.

posts.headline: March 22: 13 Years Since Bad Religion
posts.prose: I remember walking into the 9:30 Club that March night in 2013, thirteen years ago now, and feeling like I was stepping into punk rock church. Bad Religion delivered their signature blend of melody and fury to a packed room, with Against Me!, The Bronx, and Polar Bear Club warming up the crowd beforehand. The whole evening felt like a masterclass in how punk has evolved since Bad Religion formed back in 1979, yet Greg Graffin's voice cut through the years like nothing had changed. Sometimes the best shows are the ones that remind you why you fell in love with live music in the first place.

social.hook: Three openers, one headliner, and Greg Graffin's voice unchanged across three decades.
social.caption: Bad Religion turned the 9:30 Club into punk rock church that night, with Against Me!, The Bronx, and Polar Bear Club setting the table. Some shows remind you exactly why you started going to shows.
beats: Four bands on one bill: Polar Bear Club, The Bronx, Against Me!, and Bad Religion closing it out.
Each opener raised the temperature in the room before Graffin ever stepped to the mic.
Bad Religion formed in 1979 — by 2013 that was thirty-four years of melody and fury refined to a point.
Graffin's voice carried the whole room without a hint of distance from the records.
The 9:30 Club packed, the set a reminder of what drew me to live music in the first place.

posts.headline: Blancmange: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: I saw Blancmange exactly once in 38 years of concertgoing — April 15, 1986 at Crawford Hall in Irvine — and somehow never crossed paths with them again. This English synth-pop duo formed in 1979 and had albums like "Happy Families" and "Mange Tout" in their catalog, yet they became the ultimate one-and-done in my concert history. It's fascinating how some artists slip through your life just once, leaving you with a single snapshot of a moment that never repeated itself.

social.hook: 38 years of shows. One night with Blancmange. That's all there was.
social.caption: Blancmange crossed my path exactly once in nearly four decades of concertgoing. One night, one snapshot, never repeated.
beats: In 38 years of concertgoing, only one night ever belonged to Blancmange.
They'd already released 'Happy Families' and 'Mange Tout' by the time I caught them at Crawford Hall.
The English synth-pop duo formed in 1979 — a whole history packed into a single April evening for me.
Every other artist I loved, I found again. Blancmange I found once and never recovered.
The archive holds thousands of nights. This is the one that never got a sequel.

posts.headline: March 23: 21 Years Since Social Distortion
posts.prose: I caught Social Distortion at the Hard Rock Hotel in Las Vegas on March 23, 2005, and I still remember how surreal it felt seeing Mike Ness's tattooed storytelling in that glitzy casino setting. Twenty-one years later, that show stands out as one of those perfect mismatches — punk rock grit against Vegas excess, like hearing "White Light White Heat White Trash" while slot machines chimed in the distance. There's something beautifully defiant about Social Distortion that made even more sense in that artificial paradise.

social.hook: Slot machines chiming somewhere behind 'White Light White Heat White Trash.'
social.caption: Social Distortion in a casino ballroom is a mismatch that somehow made perfect sense. Mike Ness's tattooed defiance hit different against all that manufactured glamour.
beats: The Hard Rock Hotel Las Vegas, 2005 — not the obvious room for punk rock grit.
Mike Ness played 'White Light White Heat White Trash' while slot machines chimed somewhere in the distance.
That tension between the song and the setting wasn't ironic — it made the defiance feel louder.
Twenty-one years on, it's still the show I reach for when someone asks what 'perfect mismatch' means.

posts.headline: Tears For Fears: 17 Years Between Shows
posts.prose: I remember walking out of the Universal Amphitheater in 2005 after Tears For Fears, thinking it might be the last time I'd see Roland Orzabal and Curt Smith together on stage. Seventeen years later, I found myself at the Kia Forum in Inglewood, watching them perform like no time had passed at all. The gap between those shows spans nearly two decades of my life — jobs, moves, relationships — but hearing "Mad World" again felt like stepping back into that younger version of myself. Four shows total across all these years, and somehow each one marked a different chapter of growing up with their music.

posts.headline: Erasure — Days Before Violator Dropped
posts.prose: March 1990 was the moment synth-pop split into two futures — one heading for the dancefloor, the other for the stadium. I caught Erasure at the Forum just 8 days before Depeche Mode's Violator dropped, unknowingly witnessing the last gasps of pure pop innocence before their darker cousins conquered the world. Andy Bell's voice soared through "A Little Respect" while somewhere across town, Dave Gahan was probably rehearsing "Personal Jesus" for arenas that would dwarf this moment. Sometimes the most significant concerts are the ones that capture a scene right before it changes forever.

social.hook: Eight days before Violator landed, synth-pop still belonged to the dancefloor.
social.caption: I saw Erasure at the Forum on March 11, 1990 — eight days before the world changed. Andy Bell's voice carried 'A Little Respect' through a room that had no idea what was coming.
beats: March 1990: synth-pop was splitting in two, and most of us hadn't noticed yet.
Andy Bell filled the Forum with 'A Little Respect' — pure pop, no shadows, no pretense.
Eight days later, Violator dropped and Depeche Mode claimed the stadiums.
That night in Inglewood now reads like the last frame before the cut.
The archive exists for exactly this: concerts that only made sense in hindsight.

posts.headline: The Alarm: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: I caught The Alarm exactly once in my entire concert-going life — April 12, 1986 at UCLA — and somehow never circled back to them again across nearly four decades of shows. This Welsh alternative rock band, formed in 1981, was riding high on their Strength album when I saw them, yet they became a complete one-and-done in my archive despite releasing Eye of the Hurricane the following year. It's genuinely puzzling how a band can make enough of an impression to get me to a show, then vanish entirely from my radar for the next 38 years.

social.hook: One show in 38 years of concert-going, and I still can't explain why.
social.caption: The Alarm made enough of an impression to get me through the door at UCLA in 1986 — then disappeared from my radar for nearly four decades. One show, zero returns, no good explanation.
beats: The Alarm were a Welsh alternative rock band formed in 1981, and by April 1986 they had real momentum behind them.
Their album Strength was the reason I was in that room — it was the current record, and it was working on me.
The show landed. I remember going. What I can't reconstruct is why I never went back.
Eye of the Hurricane came out the following year. I didn't show up for that tour, or any tour after.
38 years of shows since that night, and this is the only entry The Alarm gets in the archive.

posts.headline: Echo and the Bunnymen: 26 Years Between Shows
posts.prose: I caught Echo and the Bunnymen at Irvine Meadows in 1984, when their post-punk atmospherics still felt urgent and new. Twenty-six years passed before I saw them again — a quarter-century gap that took me from California amphitheaters to a cramped club in D.C. called The Black Cat in 2010. By then, Ian McCulloch's voice had weathered but the songs from *Porcupine* and those early albums still carried that same moody weight. Sometimes the longest waits between shows make you appreciate how certain bands become part of your internal soundtrack, whether you're actively listening or not.

social.hook: Twenty-six years between shows, and Porcupine still hit the same nerve.
social.caption: I saw Echo & the Bunnymen at Irvine Meadows in 1984, then not again until a cramped D.C. club in 2010. A quarter-century gap taught me how certain songs live in you whether you tend to them or not.
beats: September 1984: Echo & the Bunnymen at Irvine Meadows, post-punk atmospherics that felt urgent and genuinely new.
Then nothing — twenty-six years of the songs living somewhere in the background of everything else.
The Black Cat in Washington D.C., 2010: a cramped club, a world away from a California amphitheater.

posts.headline: No Doubt — Days Before It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back Dropped
posts.prose: Hip-hop was about to get its political manifesto, but I was watching a ska band from Orange County play at the happiest place on earth. While Chuck D was putting the finishing touches on hip-hop's first true political landmark, I was experiencing the early stirrings of what would become the ska revival, watching Gwen Stefani and company work through their sound in front of families with mouse ears. posts.headline: The Brian Setzer Orchestra — Days After The Bends Dropped
posts.prose: March 1995 was a pivotal moment in rock history — Radiohead had just released The Bends, the album that signaled they were doing something different from everyone else, and I found myself at the Hard Rock Cafe in Newport Beach just 13 days later watching The Brian Setzer Orchestra swing through their rockabilly revival. While Thom Yorke was pushing guitar music into uncharted emotional territory, I was experiencing the opposite impulse: Brian Setzer's calculated nostalgia, all pompadour and upright bass, pulling rock back to its 1950s roots. posts.headline: Social Distortion + 14 More: 2018 Festival Bill
posts.prose: California punk's founding fathers assembled for what felt like a family reunion at Huntington State Beach in 2018, with Social Distortion, Bad Religion, and 13 other acts spanning four decades of West Coast rebellion. I didn't plan a 39-year relationship with his catalog. I just kept buying tickets.
Six shows, multiple decades, Orange County to Inglewood — the same earnest optimism each time.
Some artists earn a place in your personal soundtrack and simply never leave it.

posts.headline: Maxi Priest + 6 More: 1991 Festival Bill
posts.prose: This was reggae's moment in American mainstream consciousness, and I caught a perfect snapshot of it at Pacific Amphitheatre in June 1991. Maxi Priest was riding high with crossover hits, headlining over a seven-artist bill that included Dennis Brown and Andrew Tosh — Peter Tosh's son, carrying forward his father's legacy. I remember the crowd being surprisingly diverse for Orange County, drawn by reggae's growing radio presence around that time. What struck me most was how the music unified this massive outdoor crowd, from the opening act through Priest's closing set under the California stars.

social.hook: Seven artists, one California night, and reggae had never felt more mainstream
social.caption: Dennis Brown and Andrew Tosh were on the same bill the night Maxi Priest headlined Pacific Amphitheatre. Orange County crowds were not supposed to look like that, but this one did.

From the opening act through Maxi Priest's closing set, the amphitheatre held together as one.
I was there for the snapshot. The archive has the full picture.

posts.headline: Social Distortion: 34 Years of Shows
posts.prose: I first caught Social Distortion at Cal State Fullerton in 1990, back when Mike Ness was still carving out that distinctive sound that would define them through White Light White Heat White Trash and beyond. Eight shows across 34 years might not sound like devotion, but with Social D, each one felt like checking in with an old friend who'd weathered the same storms. My most recent show was just this past December at The Belasco, and hearing those same punk rock anthems that shaped my college years still hit with the same raw honesty. There's something comforting about a band that refuses to reinvent itself—they just keep getting better at being exactly who they've always been.

social.hook: Eight shows, 34 years, and every one felt like checking in.
social.caption: I've seen Social Distortion eight times across 34 years, from Cal State Fullerton in 1990 to The Belasco this past December. The raw honesty never left the room.
beats: September 1990: my first Social D show, and Mike Ness was already playing like he had nothing left to prove.

They never reinvented themselves. They just kept getting better at being exactly who they always were.
All eight nights are in the archive — the dates, the details, the reason I keep going back.

posts.headline: Oingo Boingo + 5 More: 1987 Festival Bill
posts.prose: This was the era when alternative rock was still finding its footing alongside new wave's final flourishes — and somehow I caught all of it on one stage in Tijuana. Six acts that would define different corners of the late-80s landscape: Oingo Boingo riding high on "Dead Man's Party," The Bangles at their commercial peak, Squeeze's sophisticated pop craft, and Australia's Hoodoo Gurus bringing their garage rock energy just five years after forming. I remember the surreal border-crossing pilgrimage to Caliente Racetrack, where Chris Isaak's crooning and The Fixx's synth-rock completed this unlikely but perfect snapshot of 1987's musical diversity. Looking back, it feels like witnessing a changing of the guard I didn't even know was happening.

social.hook: Six bands, one racetrack, one border crossing I'll never forget
social.caption: Six acts on one stage at a racetrack in Tijuana — Oingo Boingo, The Bangles, Squeeze, and three more. A single afternoon that felt like a survey of everything alternative rock was becoming.
beats: June 30, 1987: crossing the border to catch six bands at a horse racing venue felt absurd. It wasn't.
Oingo Boingo, The Bangles, and Squeeze alone would have been enough. Then add Chris Isaak, The Fixx, and Hoodoo Gurus.
Hoodoo Gurus had only formed five years earlier. Somehow they belonged on that stage as much as anyone.
Chris Isaak's croon next to The Fixx's synths next to garage rock — the bill shouldn't have worked. It did.
I didn't know I was watching a changing of the guard. That's usually how those moments go.

posts.headline: Crowded House: From Opener to Headliner
posts.prose: Crowded House's trajectory from Melbourne alt-rock darlings to enduring pop craftsmen spans exactly the 30 years between when I saw them open for Peter Gabriel at the Olympic Velodrome in 1993 and headline The Wiltern in 2023. That first show came around the time *Woodface* had established them as more than just Neil Finn's post-Split Enz project, but they were still very much the supporting act in a massive arena. Three decades later, watching them command their own stage at the Wiltern felt like witnessing the full arc of a band that never chased trends but simply outlasted them. Some artists earn their headliner status through persistence and craft rather than flash.

social.hook: Thirty years from opening act to headliner — the long way around.
social.caption: Crowded House opened for Peter Gabriel in 1993; thirty years later they headlined the Wiltern. Some bands earn it through persistence and craft rather than flash.
beats: September 1993: Crowded House were still the opening act, warming up an arena for Peter Gabriel.
Woodface had already landed, but Neil Finn's band was proving itself beyond the Split Enz shadow.
They never chased the trend that was coming or the one after that — they just kept making the songs.
The Wiltern, 2023: same band, their own stage, thirty years of proof behind every note.
The full arc of it only makes sense if you were at both ends.

posts.headline: My West Coast Chapter: 26 Concerts Over 11 Years
posts.prose: I still remember standing at Irvine Meadows in October 1988, watching Oingo Boingo tear through the night air, thinking I had no idea what the next 11 years of California shows would look like. That first West Coast concert cracked something open — 26 shows across 16 venues, from Irvine to Redondo Beach, two full decades bleeding into each other. I caught 22 different artists during that chapter, ending quietly at Club Caprice in 1999 with Alien Fashion Show, which is honestly a perfect last entry for a run that started with Oingo Boingo. Some chapters close before you realize they've closed.

social.hook: 26 shows, 16 venues, 22 artists — and I didn't know it had started yet.
social.caption: I was standing at Irvine Meadows in October 1988 with no idea I'd just opened an 11-year California chapter. It closed in 1999 at Club Caprice with Alien Fashion Show.

It ended quietly in 1999 — Club Caprice, Alien Fashion Show, no fanfare.
Some chapters close before you realize they've closed. This one finally has a cover.

posts.headline: Squeeze: From Opener to Headliner
posts.prose: Few bands embodied the scrappy spirit of new wave quite like Squeeze, and my concert history accidentally documented their long climb from opening act to headliner. I first saw them opening for Oingo Boingo at a racetrack in Tijuana in 1987, when their clever wordplay and pub rock energy felt perfectly suited to warming up a crowd. Twenty-five years later, I watched them headline Rams Head Live in Baltimore, now seasoned veterans commanding the stage with the same wit but deeper confidence. It's rare to witness that complete arc in your own concert diary — from promising opener to rightful headliner.

social.caption: My first Squeeze show was a support slot at a racetrack in Tijuana in 1987. Twenty-five years later I watched them headline — same wit, different footing.

Twenty-five years on, I watched them headline Rams Head Live in Baltimore, the same band with a different gravity.
It's rare to hold both ends of an arc in your own concert diary — the promising opener and the rightful headliner.

posts.headline: Tears For Fears: 37 Years of Shows
posts.prose: I remember discovering Tears For Fears at Pacific Amphitheatre in 1985, when "Songs from the Big Chair" was still fresh and Roland Orzabal's voice felt like it could crack open the world. Four shows across 37 years might not seem like much, but each one marked a different chapter of my life — from that first encounter in Costa Mesa to their triumphant return at the Kia Forum in 2022. What strikes me most is how their pop-rock has aged: the synthesizers that once felt futuristic now carry the weight of memory, and those soaring choruses hit differently when you've lived through four decades of hearing them. Some artists you grow out of; others grow with you.

posts.headline: Universal Amphitheater: 5 Shows Over 3 Decades
posts.prose: I remember discovering the Universal Amphitheater through Howard Jones in 1989, drawn by those sweeping synthesizer melodies and his earnest pop optimism. Something about that venue kept pulling me back — the way it nestled into the Hollywood Hills, intimate enough to feel personal but grand enough for proper spectacle. Over 16 years, I caught 5 shows there across three decades, from Siouxsie and the Banshees' dark glamour to The Brian Setzer Orchestra's rockabilly swagger, ending with Tears For Fears in 2005. It became my accidental home base for catching acts that mattered to me, though I didn't realize I was building a pattern until I looked back at the ticket stubs.

social.hook: Five shows. Sixteen years. I didn't know it was a pattern until I found the stubs.
social.caption: Five shows at the same venue across three decades — Howard Jones to Tears for Fears — and I never planned any of it. The ticket stubs told me the story before I did.

Over 16 years I kept returning: Siouxsie's dark glamour, Brian Setzer's rockabilly swagger, and others in between.
I didn't think of it as a home base until I laid the stubs out and counted five shows across three decades.
Tears for Fears closed it out in 2005 — sixteen years after it started, still the same accidental pull.

posts.headline: Irvine Meadows: 16 Shows Over 3 Decades
posts.prose: I discovered Irvine Meadows on April 27, 1984, watching Adam Ant command that massive outdoor stage under the California sun. Something about that amphitheater just clicked — the way sound carried across those concrete terraces, how the San Gabriel Mountains framed every performance. Over the next 19 years, I kept coming back, catching everyone from Thompson Twins to Billy Idol to my final show there with Peter Gabriel in 2003. Sixteen concerts spanning three decades at one venue feels almost accidental until you realize it wasn't — some places just become part of your concert DNA.

social.hook: Sixteen shows at one amphitheater, starting the day I figured out it was mine.
social.caption: From Adam Ant in 1984 to Peter Gabriel in 2003, Irvine Meadows quietly became the spine of my concert life. Nineteen years, thirteen artists, one stage framed by the San Gabriel Mountains.
beats: April 27, 1984: Adam Ant on that big outdoor stage was my first look at what Irvine Meadows could do.
The concrete terraces carried sound in a way I didn't find anywhere else in Southern California.
Thompson Twins, Depeche Mode, New Order, Duran Duran — the 80s ran through this one venue like a thread.
George Michael, Oingo Boingo, Erasure, Jimmy Buffett: the 90s stretched the room without changing what made it work.
Peter Gabriel closed it out for me in 2003. Sixteen shows. It was never accidental.

posts.headline: Kia Forum: 5 Shows Over 3 Decades
posts.prose: I remember walking into the Forum for the first time in 1990 to see Erasure, that massive bowl of a venue feeling both intimate and overwhelming at 19 years old. Five shows across 33 years have brought me back to Inglewood — from Bell Biv DeVoe's New Jack Swing energy to Elton John's piano grandeur to Tears for Fears' nostalgic pull. My most recent visit was Depeche Mode in 2023, and I realized I've been loyal to this place longer than some of my friendships. There's something about the Forum's acoustics that makes every synthesizer sound like it's coming from the future.

social.caption: I first walked into that massive bowl of a venue at 19, and five shows across 33 years have made it one of the most constant places in my life. Depeche Mode in 2023 closed the loop — for now.

Tears for Fears made the room feel nostalgic for something I couldn't quite name.
